title: Hymn and Smile
premise: Wren Winterbourne, a meticulous property surveyor, is hired to appraise the decaying Halloway farmhouse and discovers that every photograph taken inside now contains an extra chair — a chair that moves closer to the camera each day. The house was built by founders of a vanished congregation who bound a vengeful spirit into its walls through an unfinished ritual, and Wren's own grandmother was the last keeper who fled before completing it. As Wren documents the house's escalating hauntings alongside the ragtag neighbors who become his found family, he learns the ritual can only be finished by someone with Winterbourne blood — but finishing it means either freeing the spirit to take its long-delayed vengeance or binding it forever at the cost of his own memory. In the end, Wren chooses a third path: he testifies. He reads the founders' crimes aloud in the house's parlor, giving the spirit the justice the law never provided, and the chair finally stands empty.
about_author: Petra Kavanagh is a former rural assessor from western Pennsylvania whose decade of inspecting abandoned properties left her with a folder of photographs she refuses to look at after dark. She writes horror about paperwork, inheritance, and the houses that remember more than their owners do.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren arrives at the Halloway farmhouse to appraise it for a bank sale, documenting every room with methodical care. He notes odd architectural details: a sealed parlor, thirteen doors for ten rooms. Emotional beat: professional detachment masking loneliness, establishing documentation as his coping ritual.

chapters.title: Thirteen Doors
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Measuring the house, Wren counts thirteen interior doors but can only ever find twelve at a time; his floor plans redraw themselves overnight. A neighbor, Odile, warns him off the property. Emotional beat: first crack in his rational worldview, unease sharpening into obsession.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Album
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Sorting his late grandmother's belongings, Wren finds her old photos of the same house — and in every one, an extra wooden chair sits where none should be. Her handwriting labels one photo 'the thirteenth door is a person.' Emotional beat: grief entangling with dread as family history turns sinister.

chapters.title: Odile and the Others
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile introduces Wren to her circle: ex-deacon Marcus, teenage runaway Sef, and archivist Ruthie, who have quietly tracked the house's history for years. They reveal the founders' congregation vanished in 1911. Emotional beat: wary connection; Wren resists belonging even as he's drawn in.

chapters.title: What the Deed Says
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. In county archives, Ruthie finds the original deed requiring 'a seat be kept' for an unnamed party, plus records of a 1911 death the coroner refused to certify. The founders bound something after a killing they committed themselves. Emotional beat: the theme of justice outside the law takes root.

chapters.title: Closer Every Day
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren's new photographs of the house show the extra chair advancing toward the camera — inches per day. He begins sleeping in his car. Sef, squatting nearby, sees the chair physically manifest on the porch. Emotional beat: mounting terror; documentation stops being comfort and becomes evidence of doom.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Confession
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Hidden in grandmother's Bible, Wren finds her unfinished letter: she was the appointed keeper, tasked with completing the founders' ritual, and she fled rather than choose between binding the spirit or freeing it. Emotional beat: betrayal and inheritance collide; Wren realizes he was summoned by bloodline, not coincidence.

chapters.title: Sitting Down
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus, seeking absolution for his own church failures, enters the house alone and is found seated in the extra chair, catatonic, mouthing testimony no one can hear. Emotional beat: loyalty tested against truth — the group must decide whether saving Marcus means entering the house.

chapters.title: Rules of Evidence
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Ruthie deciphers the ritual text: the spirit, Eli Voss, was murdered by the founders after witnessing their crimes, and the ritual requires a full accounting read aloud in the parlor — then a choice: bind or release. Emotional beat: hope with a price tag; knowledge becomes responsibility.

chapters.title: The Bank Calls
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren's employer demands his appraisal; the bank wants the house cleared by month's end, threatening demolition — which would free Eli unbound. Time pressure crystallizes. Emotional beat: institutional indifference versus personal duty; Wren falsifies nothing for once and stalls instead.

chapters.title: Sef's Night Watch
chapters.summary: Sef's POV. Sef keeps vigil over catatonic Marcus and witnesses the chair appear in the safehouse, having followed them. Sef realizes distance doesn't exist for the house. Emotional beat: fear transmuted into fierce protectiveness; the found family tightens its circle.

chapters.title: Winterbourne Blood
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The ritual text specifies the reader must carry the keeper's blood. Wren tests himself against the house: doors open before he touches them. He admits to the group what completion might cost him — his memories, possibly his self. Emotional beat: reluctant acceptance of being chosen.

chapters.title: Bind or Burn
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The group fractures: Marcus's sister demands they bind Eli forever to end the danger; Ruthie argues releasing him is justice; Odile fears any choice kills someone. Emotional beat: loyalty versus truth made explicit — the family argues not whether to act, but what they owe a victim.

chapters.title: The Parlor Opens
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The sealed parlor unlocks itself, revealing the founders' crime scene preserved mid-century: ledgers, a bloodstain, Eli's belongings labeled like evidence never filed. Wren photographs everything. Emotional beat: awe and revulsion; the house has been waiting for a witness all along.

chapters.title: Testimony of the Dead
chapters.summary: Eli's POV (first break from the living). Eli's fragmentary consciousness recalls his murder and century of watching keepers flee. He does not want vengeance — he wants the record corrected. Emotional beat: the monster revealed as plaintiff; sympathy destabilizes the group's plans.

chapters.title: Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The bank schedules demolition in four days, and a crew arrives early to survey. The house defends itself; a worker is injured, and Wren takes the blame to buy time, jeopardizing his career. Emotional beat: sacrifice; Wren burns his respectable life to protect the work.

chapters.title: What Marcus Saw
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus surfaces from catatonia with Eli's full account memorized: names, dates, the location of Eli's remains under the parlor floor. Speaking it nearly unmakes him. Emotional beat: truth as burden; the group now holds evidence no court will ever hear.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. On the final night, the group gathers in the parlor and Wren reads the complete accounting aloud — the founders' crimes, the cover-up, the coroner's refusal — while the house shakes and the chair draws near. Emotional beat: climax of voice; documentation becomes liturgy, prayer fulfilled as testimony.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Offered the choice — bind or release — Wren instead offers Eli what neither option contained: acknowledgment, a named grave, and the record entered into the world outside the house. The chair empties. The thirteenth door opens onto morning. Emotional beat: catharsis; justice rendered without law or sacrifice.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Documented
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. The house stands ordinary, twelve doors, no chair. Ruthie files Eli's story in the archive under his own name. Marcus recovers slowly; Sef stays with Odile. Emotional beat: quiet repair; the found family remains, bonded by what they witnessed together.

chapters.title: Appraisal Revised
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren submits a final report valuing the house at exactly what it's worth and resigns, keeping only his photographs — in which the chair appears one last time, empty, by a window in sunlight. Emotional beat: peace earned; he keeps documenting, but now as remembrance rather than fear.

chapters.title: Hymn and Smile
chapters.summary: Ensemble epilogue. Months later, the group visits Eli's marked grave with flowers and a sung hymn; Sef smiles for the first time in the narrative. A new photograph shows nothing out of place. Final line echoes grandma's album: some houses only ever wanted to be heard. Emotional beat: resolution, gratitude, and gentle vigilance.
